newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: C/a deficit shows confidence in NZ growth - Peters.
newsitem.headline: C/a deficit shows confidence in NZ growth - Peters.

text.p: New Zealand's current account deficit is climbing as a result of private domestic and foreign investors' confidence in the country's growth potential, Treasurer Winston Peters said on Wednesday.
The growing deficit was not the product of a spend-thrift government, he told Bay of Plenty business leaders at a lunch in Tauranga.
"We have no cause for concern when money is being borrowed to produce productivity," Peters said.
"Government spending on consumption, once a major driving force in New Zealand's current account deficit, is no longer a factor. We have got our act together."
Peters said economic growth was expected to average around 3.0 to 3.5 percent annually over the next three years, and the government expects to achieve on-going surpluses.

The government's December Economic and Fiscal Update forecast the current account balance would peak at $4.9 billion (4.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product) in the March 1999 year, before falling to $4.0 billion by March 2000.
Statistics New Zealand said the deficit was $4.2 billion in the September 1996 year, 4.6 percent of GDP.
